title: Functions
description: Function notation, domain and range, composite and inverse functions, and graph transformations

notes.heading: Function Notation, Domain and Range
notes.body:
A **function** $f$ assigns exactly one output to each input. We write $f: x \mapsto f(x)$, and the set of allowed inputs is the **domain**; the set of outputs actually produced is the **range**.

📌 **Definition** — $f(a)$ is the **value** of $f$ at $x = a$; the graph of $f$ is the set of all points $(x, f(x))$ with $x$ in the domain.

💡 **Worked Example** — For $f(x) = x^2 - 4x$ with domain $x \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$f(3) = 9 - 12 = -3$$
Completing the square, $f(x) = (x-2)^2 - 4$, so the range is $f(x) \ge -4$.

🔑 Domain is an *input* question and range is an *output* question. When a question says "state the range", find the highest or lowest point of the graph and check whether the curve closes up or runs to infinity.

notes.heading: Finding the Domain from a Formula
notes.body:
When no domain is given, the domain is every real number for which the formula produces a real output. Two features break it:

• A **denominator** must not be zero.
• An **even root** (square root, fourth root) must not take a negative argument.

💡 **Worked Example** — Find the domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x+1}}{x-3}$.
The root needs $x + 1 \ge 0$, so $x \ge -1$. The denominator forbids $x = 3$. Together:
$$x \ge -1, \quad x \ne 3$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Writing $x \ne 3$ only, or letting the square root rule vanish once a second condition is added. Every restriction the formula imposes must survive.

📌 For a logarithm the argument must be strictly positive: the domain of $\ln(5 - x)$ is $x < 5$.

notes.heading: Composite Functions
notes.body:
Applying $g$ then $f$ gives the **composite** $f \circ g$, defined by
$$(f \circ g)(x) = f\big(g(x)\big)$$
The function nearest the $x$ acts first: $f \circ g$ is *"$g$ first, then $f$"*.

💡 **Worked Example** — With $f(x) = 2x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$:
$$(f \circ g)(x) = f(x^2) = 2x^2 + 1 \qquad (g \circ f)(x) = g(2x+1) = (2x+1)^2$$

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Assuming $f \circ g = g \circ f$. They are different functions in general, and the two above are a counter-example.

📌 A composite is only defined where the inner function is defined *and* its output is allowed by the outer function. For $(f \circ g)(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-2}$ with $g(x) = x + 2$, the value $x = 0$ is excluded even though the formula simplifies neatly.

notes.heading: Inverse Functions
notes.body:
The inverse $f^{-1}$ undoes $f$: it sends each output back to the input that produced it. It exists exactly when $f$ is **one-to-one** — no horizontal line meets the graph twice.

**Finding the inverse takes three steps:** write $y = f(x)$; interchange $x$ and $y$; solve for $y$.

💡 **Worked Example** — $f(x) = 3x - 5$.
$$y = 3x - 5 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = 3y - 5 \;\Longrightarrow\; y = \dfrac{x+5}{3}$$
so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x+5}{3}$. Check: $f^{-1}(f(4)) = f^{-1}(7) = 4$ ✓

🔑 The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, and the range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$. The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$.

⚠️ $f^{-1}(x)$ means the inverse function, never the reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.

notes.heading: Transformations: Translations and Reflections
notes.body:
Starting from a known graph $y = f(x)$, the common transformations are:

• $y = f(x) + a$ — translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ a \end{pmatrix}$ (up for $a > 0$).
• $y = f(x - a)$ — translation by $\begin{pmatrix} a \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$ (**right** for $a > 0$).
• $y = -f(x)$ — reflection in the $x$-axis.
• $y = f(-x)$ — reflection in the $y$-axis.

💡 **Worked Example** — The graph of $y = f(x)$ passes through $(4, 3)$. Then:
• $y = f(x) + 5$ passes through $(4, 8)$.
• $y = f(x - 2)$ passes through $(6, 3)$.
• $y = -f(x)$ passes through $(4, -3)$.

⚠️ **Common mistake** — Reading $f(x - 2)$ as a shift to the left. Inside the bracket the transformation acts *opposite* to the sign, because the new graph needs the **larger** input $x = 6$ to reuse the old output $f(4)$.

illustration.alt: Four panels showing the graph of a function drawn dashed beside y = f(x) + 2 shifted up, y = f(x − 2) shifted right, y = −f(x) reflected in the x-axis and y = 2f(x) stretched vertically.
illustration.caption: Stretches and reflections act on the outside and behave as written; a change inside the bracket moves the graph the opposite way.

notes.heading: Transformations: Stretches
notes.body:
Two stretches complete the toolkit:

• $y = a\,f(x)$ — **vertical** stretch, scale factor $a$, away from the $x$-axis. The $y$-coordinates are multiplied by $a$.
• $y = f(kx)$ — **horizontal** stretch, scale factor $\dfrac{1}{k}$, away from the $y$-axis. The $x$-coordinates are divided by $k$.

💡 **Worked Example** — The graph of $y = f(x)$ has a maximum at $(2, 6)$.
• $y = 3f(x)$ has a maximum at $(2, 18)$.
• $y = f(2x)$ has a maximum at $(1, 6)$.

🔑 Vertical changes act on the outside (on $y$) and do exactly what they say. Horizontal changes act on the inside (on $x$) and do the **inverse**: $f(2x)$ squashes the graph to half its width.

📌 When several transformations are combined, apply them in the order the expression is built up from $f(x)$.

notes.heading: Rational Graphs, Asymptotes and Exam Technique
notes.body:
For $y = \dfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}$ the graph has a **vertical asymptote** where the denominator is zero and a **horizontal asymptote** at $y = \dfrac{a}{c}$, found by dividing both terms by the highest power of $x$.

💡 **Worked Example** — $y = \dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$.
• Denominator zero: $x = 3$ is the vertical asymptote.
• Large $x$: dividing top and bottom by $x$ gives $\dfrac{2 + \frac1x}{1 - \frac3x} \to 2$, so $y = 2$ is the horizontal asymptote.

**Checklist for sketching**
• Find the intercepts: $x = 0$ for the $y$-intercept, $y = 0$ for the $x$-intercept.
• Mark the asymptotes as dashed lines and state them.
• Sketch the two branches, which sit on opposite sides of the vertical asymptote.

⚠️ **Common mistakes** — Joining the two branches across an asymptote; forgetting that the graph is undefined at the vertical asymptote; assuming the horizontal asymptote is a value the curve reaches.

questions.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = 3x - 2$. Find $f(5)$.
What is the domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-4}$?
questions.explanation: The denominator is zero at $x = 4$, so that single value is excluded: the domain is all real $x$ with $x \ne 4$.

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = x^2$ has domain $x \in \mathbb{R}$. State its range.
questions.explanation: A square is never negative and every non-negative value is attained, so the range is $y \ge 0$.

questions.stem: Given $f(x) = 2x$ and $g(x) = x + 3$, find $f\big(g(1)\big)$.
questions.explanation: The inner function acts first: $g(1) = 4$, then $f(4) = 2 \times 4 = 8$.

questions.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = 4x - 7$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.explanation: Interchange $x$ and $y$ in $y = 4x - 7$ to get $x = 4y - 7$, then $y = \dfrac{x+7}{4}$, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x+7}{4}$. Check: $f^{-1}(f(2)) = f^{-1}(1) = 2$ ✓

questions.stem: Given $f(x) = x^2 - 3$ and $g(x) = x + 1$, find $(f \circ g)(x)$.
Find the domain of $f(x) = \sqrt{2x - 6}$.
questions.explanation: The expression under the square root must be non-negative: $2x - 6 \ge 0$ gives $x \ge 3$.

questions.stem: The graph of $y = f(x - 2)$ is the graph of $y = f(x)$ translated
questions.explanation: Replacing $x$ by $x - 2$ shifts the graph 2 units to the right: the new graph needs the larger input $x = 2$ to reuse the old value $f(0)$.

questions.stem: Which of these functions is its own inverse?
questions.explanation: For $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ the interchange step returns the same formula, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{x} = f(x)$. The others are not self-inverse.

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = \sqrt{x-1}$ has domain $x \ge 1$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$, stating its domain.
questions.explanation: From $y = \sqrt{x-1}$ we get $y^2 = x - 1$, so $x = y^2 + 1$ and $f^{-1}(x) = x^2 + 1$. Its domain is the range of $f$, which is $x \ge 0$ (a square root is never negative).

questions.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x-2}$, $x \ne 2$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.explanation: Write $y = \dfrac{x}{x-2}$, so $y(x-2) = x$, giving $yx - x = 2y$ and $x(y-1) = 2y$. Hence $x = \dfrac{2y}{y-1}$ and $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{2x}{x-1}$.

questions.stem: The graph of $y = f(x)$ passes through the point $(3, 4)$. Which point lies on the graph of $y = 2f(x) + 1$?
questions.explanation: The $x$-coordinate is unchanged because the transformation acts on the outside. The new $y$-coordinate is $2(4) + 1 = 9$, so the point is $(3, 9)$.

questions.stem: The graph of $y = f(x)$ has a maximum point at $(4, 7)$. Find the maximum point of the graph of $y = f\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)$.
questions.explanation: Replacing $x$ by $\dfrac{x}{2}$ stretches the graph horizontally with scale factor 2, so the $x$-coordinate doubles to 8 while the $y$-coordinate is unchanged: $(8, 7)$.

questions.stem: Given $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-2}$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x+2}$, state the domain of the composite $f \circ g$.
questions.explanation:
$(f \circ g)(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+2}-2}$. The root requires $x \ge -2$ and the denominator requires $\sqrt{x+2} 
e 2$, which squares to $x + 2 
e 4$ and hence $x 
e 2$. Both restrictions apply, so the domain is $x \ge -2$ with $x 
e 2$.

questions.stem: State the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $y = \dfrac{2x+1}{x-3}$.
questions.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by $x$: $\dfrac{2 + \frac1x}{1 - \frac3x} \to \dfrac{2}{1} = 2$ as $x \to \infty$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y = 2$. (The vertical asymptote is $x = 3$.)

questions.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = x^2 + 2x$. Find $f(3)$.
What is the domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{3}{x+5}$?
questions.explanation: The denominator is zero at $x = -5$, so that single value is excluded: the domain is all real $x$ with $x \ne -5$.

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 11$ has domain $x \in \mathbb{R}$. State its range.
questions.explanation: Completing the square gives $f(x) = (x-3)^2 + 2$. The square is never negative, so the least value is $2$ and the range is $y \ge 2$.

questions.stem: Given $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = x - 2$, find $g\big(f(3)\big)$.
questions.explanation: The inner function acts first: $f(3) = 9$, then $g(9) = 9 - 2 = 7$. ($1$ applies the functions in the wrong order.)

questions.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = 2x + 3$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.explanation: Interchange $x$ and $y$ in $y = 2x + 3$ to get $x = 2y + 3$, then $y = \dfrac{x-3}{2}$, so $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x-3}{2}$. Check: $f^{-1}(f(1)) = f^{-1}(5) = 1$ ✓

questions.stem: Given $f(x) = x^2 - 2$ and $g(x) = 2x + 1$, find $(f \circ g)(x)$.
Find the domain of $f(x) = \sqrt{12 - 3x}$.
questions.explanation: The expression under the square root must be non-negative: $12 - 3x \ge 0$ gives $3x \le 12$, so $x \le 4$.

questions.stem: The graph of $y = f(x + 3)$ is the graph of $y = f(x)$ translated
questions.explanation: Replacing $x$ by $x + 3$ shifts the graph 3 units to the LEFT: the new graph reuses the old value $f(0)$ at the smaller input $x = -3$.

questions.stem: Which of these functions is its own inverse?
questions.explanation: For $f(x) = 3 - x$ the interchange step gives $x = 3 - y$, so $y = 3 - x$ again: $f^{-1} = f$. Check: $f(f(1)) = f(2) = 1$ ✓

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = x^2 - 4$ has domain $x \ge 0$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$, stating its domain.
questions.explanation: From $y = x^2 - 4$ we get $x = \sqrt{y + 4}$ (positive root, since the domain of $f$ is $x \ge 0$), so $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x+4}$. Its domain is the range of $f$, which is $y \ge -4$.

questions.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = \dfrac{x+1}{x-3}$, $x \ne 3$. Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
questions.explanation: Write $y = \dfrac{x+1}{x-3}$, so $y(x-3) = x+1$, giving $yx - x = 3y + 1$ and $x(y-1) = 3y+1$. Hence $x = \dfrac{3y+1}{y-1}$ and $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x+1}{x-1}$. Check: $f(0) = -\dfrac13$ and $f^{-1}\left(-\dfrac13\right) = 0$ ✓

questions.stem: The graph of $y = f(x)$ passes through the point $(2, 5)$. Which point lies on the graph of $y = 3f(x) - 1$?
questions.explanation: The transformation acts on the outside, so the $x$-coordinate is unchanged. The new $y$-coordinate is $3(5) - 1 = 14$, so the point is $(2, 14)$. ($16$ adds instead of subtracting; $(6, 14)$ wrongly scales $x$ too.)

questions.stem: The graph of $y = f(x)$ has a maximum point at $(6, 3)$. Find the maximum point of the graph of $y = f(3x)$.
questions.explanation: Replacing $x$ by $3x$ compresses the graph horizontally with scale factor $\dfrac13$, so the $x$-coordinate is divided by 3 while the $y$-coordinate is unchanged: $(2, 3)$.

questions.stem: Given $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-1}$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x-4}$, state the domain of the composite $f \circ g$.
questions.explanation: $(f \circ g)(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x-4}-1}$. The root requires $x \ge 4$ and the denominator requires $\sqrt{x-4} \ne 1$, which squares to $x \ne 5$. Both restrictions apply.

questions.stem: State the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $y = \dfrac{3x-2}{x+4}$.
questions.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by $x$: $\dfrac{3 - \frac2x}{1 + \frac4x} \to 3$ as $x \to \infty$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y = 3$. ($x = -4$ is the vertical asymptote.)
